subtype: Honouring a promise at a cost [Actor]
passage:
Sunday night
My arms are dead. Worth it, I think.
On Wednesday I promised Maria I'd help her move out of the PG on Sunday. Her parents are in Goa, she has no one else here, and the new flat is on the fourth floor with no lift.
Then on Friday Kunal's group got free passes to the music festival. Sunday. Front section. I stared at that message for about an hour.
I even drafted, "Maria, something came up..." Deleted it. Nothing came up. Something more fun came up. That's different.
So today I carried nineteen boxes up four floors. Maria cried a bit when we finished, sitting on the floor with a steel plate of instant noodles.
She said, "I knew you'd come. You always come." That sentence is going to stay with me longer than any festival.
Irawati

qa.q: How many boxes did Irawati carry?
qa.a: Nineteen boxes up four floors.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling while staring at the festival message?
qa.a: Irawati felt tempted and torn between the free front-section passes and the promise to Maria.

qa.q: Why was deleting the 'something came up' draft the honest choice?
qa.a: Nothing had actually come up, only something more fun, so the excuse would have been a lie; keeping the word built reliability.

qa.q: What did Irawati's help mean to Maria?
qa.a: Maria, with no one else in the city, felt relieved and cared for, crying a bit and saying 'You always come'.

grounding: Shows a young adult keeping a promise to help a friend move when a more appealing festival invite arrives, and building reliability by staying.

passage:
At break time in the school playground in Leeds, Amara pulled Fatima behind the climbing frame. "Promise you won't tell anyone? I still sleep with my old teddy. Every night."
Fatima nodded hard. "I promise."
All afternoon she felt tall and important. Amara had told her, not anyone else. But it was heavy too. When Chloe said at lunch that teddies were for babies, Fatima had to bite her lip very hard to keep quiet.
At home she asked Mum, "How do you know if you should keep a secret?"
Mum stopped chopping onions. "If it's a happy or private secret, you keep it. If it's a secret that means someone could get hurt, you tell a grown-up, even if you promised."
Fatima thought about the teddy. Nobody could get hurt by a teddy.
She kept it. She felt proud every time she saw Amara.

qa.q: What secret did Amara tell Fatima?
qa.a: Amara still sleeps with her old teddy every night.

qa.q: How did Fatima feel about being told the secret?
qa.a: Fatima felt proud and important to be trusted, but also burdened, biting her lip to keep quiet when Chloe teased about teddies.

qa.q: What rule did Mum give Fatima about secrets?
qa.a: Keep happy or private secrets, but tell a grown-up about any secret that means someone could get hurt, even after promising.

qa.q: What might it mean to Amara that Fatima kept quiet?
qa.a: Amara can feel safe and trust Fatima more, knowing a private thing was held carefully.

grounding: Shows a child proud and burdened by a friend's secret, learning to hold it while knowing that secrets about harm must go to an adult.

passage:
At the bakery after school in São Paulo, Priscila was finally sitting with the popular girls. Bea leaned in. "You're close with Layla, right? Why's she been so weird lately?"
Priscila knew why. Two weeks ago Layla had cried in the bathroom and told her, only her, that her parents were separating.
Everyone was looking at Priscila. For once she was the one who knew something.
"Her parents are getting divorced," she said. "Don't tell anyone."
For about ten seconds it felt amazing. Bea said, "Oh wow," and moved her chair closer.
By the next morning the whole class knew. Layla walked in, saw the looks, and went white. At lunch she sat alone, and when Priscila came near, she said very quietly, "I only told you."
Priscila's stomach turned over. The popular girls didn't save her a seat either.

qa.q: What had Layla told Priscila two weeks earlier?
qa.a: That her parents were separating.

qa.q: Why did Priscila tell the secret at the bakery?
qa.a: Priscila wanted to feel included and important with the popular girls, and for ten seconds being the insider felt amazing.

qa.q: What could Priscila do now to start repairing it?
qa.a: Apologise to Layla without excuses, admit it was wrong, and ask Bea and the others not to spread it further.

qa.q: What was that morning like for Layla?
qa.a: Layla felt exposed and betrayed, going white at the looks and sitting alone, since she had only told Priscila.

grounding: Shows a teenager spilling a friend's secret for a moment of closeness with others, then feeling guilty as it spreads and the friendship breaks.

In the girls' hostel of the residential school in Ooty, Lakshmi heard it from the next cubicle: "Lakshmi likes Pranav from 11B. Sachin told everyone at football."
She stood very still behind the door. She had told only one person, Sachin, her friend since Class 6, in the library last week, because he'd asked why she kept going red.
By dinner three boys hummed a love song when she passed. She laughed it off. In the dorm she pulled the blanket over her head.
For the next week she stopped sitting with Sachin at study hour. She stopped sitting with anyone. When her roommate asked what she was reading, she said, "Nothing," and turned the page.
On Friday the house mother, Mrs Joseph, found her alone on the steps. "You've gone very quiet this week. Did something happen?"
Lakshmi shrugged. Then, slowly, she told her.

qa.q: Where had Lakshmi told Sachin her secret?
qa.a: In the library last week.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after hearing the girls in the next cubicle?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt exposed and foolish, standing very still and later hiding under the blanket.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi start to open up again?
qa.a: Mrs Joseph noticing she'd gone quiet and asking gently, which gave Lakshmi a safe person to tell.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the change in Lakshmi?
qa.a: Sachin would see his friend since Class 6 stop sitting with him, and might realise how much sharing her secret hurt.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning a friend shared her secret, feeling exposed and foolish, and withdrawing from everyone afterwards.

subtype: When a secret must be told [Response]
passage:
On the school trip to Mahabaleshwar, the dorm lights went out at ten, and Tanvir whispered across the bunk. "Promise you won't tell? There's this guy online. He's twenty-four. He says I'm mature. He wants to meet when we're back, and says not to tell my parents. He's asked for photos."
Tejas's stomach went cold. "Tanvir, that's not okay. Someone who asks you to hide things from your parents isn't safe."
"You promised."
"I didn't. And this one I can't keep. I'm telling you first: I'm going to Mr Pillai. Tonight."
Rain drummed on the tin roof, and there was no signal. Tejas walked down the dark corridor and knocked until Mr Pillai opened the door.
Mr Pillai listened, then sat with both boys. "You did the right thing, Tejas. Tanvir, this is not your fault. Let's block him right now. We'll call your parents first thing when there's signal, and report the account together."

qa.q: What did the man online tell Tanvir not to do?
qa.a: Not to tell his parents.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when Tanvir described the messages?
qa.a: Tejas's stomach went cold; Tejas felt alarmed and protective, knowing a man who asks for secrecy from parents isn't safe.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that makes this the right kind of secret-breaking?
qa.a: Tejas told Tanvir first that this secret couldn't be kept, then went that night to Mr Pillai, who blocked the contact and planned to call the parents and report.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel after Mr Pillai says it's not his fault?
qa.a: Tanvir might feel embarrassed and upset with Tejas at first, but also relieved and safer, knowing adults are handling it.

grounding: Shows a teenager knowing a friend's secret about a dangerous online contact is not his to keep, telling the friend first and then a teacher that night.

Tuesday: In the hostel room, Yamini told Vasudha she hadn't slept properly in weeks and was failing two papers. "Don't tell anyone. Especially not my parents." Vasudha agreed to keep it between them and urged her to see the college counsellor. Yamini said maybe.
Friday night: Near midnight, Yamini said quietly, "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." Vasudha's heart pounded. She took Yamini's hand. "I'm staying right here with you. And I can't keep this one to myself. I'm calling the warden now." Yamini cried but didn't stop her. The warden came within ten minutes, sat with them both, and called the college counselling helpline. Someone stayed with Yamini all night.
The following Wednesday: Yamini had seen the counsellor twice. She was still a bit cross with Vasudha. But at dinner she squeezed her hand and said, "Thank you for not carrying it alone." Vasudha realised she had been holding her breath for a week.

qa.q: How soon did the warden come on Friday night?
qa.a: Within ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when Yamini spoke on Friday night?
qa.a: Vasudha's heart pounded; Vasudha felt frightened and torn about the promise, but put Yamini's safety first at once.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do on Friday night that was right?
qa.a: Stayed with Yamini, said plainly this couldn't be kept secret, and called the warden straight away, who brought in the counselling helpline that night.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel about Vasudha by the following Wednesday?
qa.a: Yamini is still a bit cross but grateful, thanking Vasudha for not carrying it alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult torn between loyalty and worry over a friend's troubles, urging help and involving qualified people at once when danger appears.

In the family's one-room flat in Dharavi, there was no door Devika could close. Her little brother Imran, six, read everything, even the diary Nani gave her for her tenth birthday. Yesterday he'd read a line out loud at dinner, and everyone laughed.
Devika's face burned. She wasn't hiding anything bad. It was just hers.
That night she asked Ammi, "Can I have a box with a lock? Just for my diary?"
Ammi frowned. "Why? What are you writing that needs a lock?"
"Nothing wrong. I just want one thing that's only mine."
Ammi looked round the crowded room. Then she nodded slowly. "Fair. We have no doors. You can have a box."
On Sunday they bought a small tin box with a tiny key. Devika wore the key on a string. Imran sulked, then asked for a box too.

qa.q: Who gave Devika the diary?
qa.a: Nani gave her the diary for her tenth birthday.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Imran read her diary at dinner?
qa.a: Devika felt embarrassed and exposed, face burning, even though there was nothing bad in it.

qa.q: How did Ammi respond in a way that respected Devika's growth?
qa.a: After asking why, Ammi listened, saw there were no doors, and agreed to a small locked box for the diary.

qa.q: How did Imran react to the box?
qa.a: Imran sulked, then asked for a box of his own.

grounding: Shows a child in a crowded home asking for a locked box for her diary, a healthy wish for privacy rather than hiding wrongdoing.

subtype: Private is not the same as hidden [Actor]
passage:
In the counsellor's room at school, Rashmi sat with her hands in her lap. Ms Rajni had asked the class to write about "private and secret" for health class, and Rashmi had stayed back.
"I keep lots of things to myself," Rashmi said. "Like my poems. Or that I miss my old school. That's just private, right?"
"Right. That's yours," Ms Rajni said.
"But there's one other thing. A college boy on a game server. He says we're special friends. He says I shouldn't tell anyone because they wouldn't get it." Rashmi looked at the floor. "That one feels different. Like I'm hiding it, not just keeping it."
Ms Rajni's voice stayed calm. "You're right. That's a secret that protects him, not you. Thank you for telling me. This isn't your fault." She moved her chair closer. "Let's block him together now, and I'll call your mother this afternoon so we can decide the next step with her."
Rashmi nodded, shaky but lighter.

qa.q: What does the college boy tell Rashmi?
qa.a: He says they're special friends and that she shouldn't tell anyone because they wouldn't get it.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel about the game-server secret?
qa.a: Rashmi felt uneasy and ashamed, sensing it was hiding rather than just keeping something private.

qa.q: What did Ms Rajni do that same day?
qa.a: Stayed calm, said it wasn't Rashmi's fault, blocked the contact with her, and planned to call Rashmi's mother that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's mother be affected by the call?
qa.a: Her mother would likely feel worried but grateful that Rashmi spoke up and that the school acted the same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager telling apart ordinary privacy from a secret that protects a risky online contact, and bringing the second to an adult.

passage:
Dear Kashish,
Now that you have your own phone, I wanted to write this down instead of making it a lecture at dinner.
Here's what I promise: I won't read your chats with your friends. Your messages, your jokes, your crushes: those are yours. I remember being fourteen.
Here's what I'll ask: the phone charges in the kitchen at night. Location sharing stays on when you go out. And if anyone online asks you to keep a secret from us, or to meet, or for photos, you tell me, and you won't be in trouble for it. Ever.
Once a week, on Sunday, let's just talk: anything weird, anything you liked, anything that worried you.
I know Bhavna aunty checks every message on Dev's phone. I'm not going to, because I'd rather you tell me things than learn to hide them better.
Love,
Mumma

qa.q: Where will the phone charge at night?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: Why does Mumma choose not to read Kashish's chats?
qa.a: Mumma would rather be trusted than spy, hoping Kashish will come to her instead of learning to hide things better.

qa.q: Which parts of the letter balance safety and privacy?
qa.a: Clear safety rules like charging in the kitchen and location sharing, a promise not to read chats, a no-trouble rule for secrecy or meeting requests, and Sunday talks.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kashish might feel respected and relieved that the chats stay private, and safer knowing anything weird can be reported without trouble.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining safety rules openly, agreeing what stays private and checking in on risk without reading every message.
